questions.stem: Use Source A in Inspect source, then answer in your exercise book.
parts: Identify the producer, population reference date, unit and what each coloured grid cell represents.
Describe two located concentrations and contrast them with a broad interior area. Name regions, not exact streets.
Identify an exception to “everyone lives on the east coast”. Use the map, not a guess.
Explain why a grey cell and a national-scale thumbnail do not prove that a place has no people, communities, activity or significance.

screens.name: Worked statistical comparison and guided source reasoning
screens.purpose: Read a properly sized table, follow a complete comparison, then plan an explanation without exposing a practice model.

workedCopy.title: Read, compare, qualify · 5 min
workedCopy.prompt: Read Source B, then follow the complete worked comparison. Why can the largest increase and the fastest growth describe different places?

steps.text: Identify: Source B is the ABS 27 March 2025 release. Its June 2024 ERP is preliminary in this dated release and may be revised later. It compares ERP for four selected GCCSAs, with changes over 2023–24. These are broad city regions, not four equally sized built-up areas.
Read: Melbourne added 142,637 residents, compared with Perth’s 72,742. Melbourne therefore had the larger numerical increase of this pair.

Calculate and compare: Melbourne’s earlier population was 5,350,705 − 142,637 = 5,208,068; 142,637 ÷ 5,208,068 × 100 ≈ 2.7%. Perth’s was 2,384,371 − 72,742 = 2,311,629; 72,742 ÷ 2,311,629 × 100 ≈ 3.1%. Perth grew faster proportionally because the change is measured against a smaller starting population.

Conclude with a limit: more added residents and a faster percentage growth are different measures. These selected city-region changes do not establish Australia’s urbanisation: a consistent urban definition and national urban/total populations over time would also be needed.

guidedCopy.title: Plan an explanation · 3 min
guidedCopy.paperInstructions: Plan four short points in your exercise book, using Sources A and B below. This is a plan, not a second full paragraph. Your teacher holds the model answer until after your attempt.

questions.stem: Explain a concentration shown on Source A.
parts: Observation: locate one concentration and contrast it with another region.
Evidence: identify the source date, what the colour represents and a relevant numerical comparison from B. Do not treat city counts as density.
Inference: propose one possible influence and explain the mechanism.
Qualification: name a missing source that could test the inference and explain one limit of A or B.

independentVariant.title: Explain one population pattern · 8 min
independentVariant.paperInstructions: Core: write 60–90 words (about four or five sentences) in your exercise book. Use 2 min to select evidence and plan, 5 min to write, and 1 min to check. Sources A and B are below. Extension, if ready: add a second possible mechanism and develop the response towards 100–140 words. Complete your attempt before teacher-led feedback.

questions.stem: How is Australia’s population distributed, and what might explain one pattern? Use Sources A and B.
parts: Describe a located distribution pattern from A and one exception.
Support your response with one accurate comparison from B, stating date/period and units.
Explain one possible influence and how it might affect the pattern. Employment, services and infrastructure are hypotheses here, not activities directly measured by A or B.
State a source limitation and propose specific additional evidence to test one explanation.
